Call the initialize API endpoint when the customer clicks the pay button, redirect them to the checkout page to complete payment, and verify it before you deliver value. It simply pings your server, and you use the returned data to deliver value to your customer. Fintech avatar ingestion with a browser-issued signed request is a boundary problem before it is a JavaScript problem. The browser sends bytes to storage; a Node.js control-plane endpoint authenticates the account, fixes the key prefix and content limits, and records a pending intent. That split avoids routing image bytes through the application, but it does not create tenant isolation by itself. Isolation comes from authorization, an unguessable key, and a post-upload check before the avatar becomes visible. My rule is simple: the signer owns policy, storage owns bytes, and the browser owns neither tenant identity nor object naming. A signed request authorizes one request shape, not a general session credential. Scanning the bundle for assets/...js paths turns up 69 unique chunk filenames, and the bundle mentions assets/ 71 times in total. items.title: EF Core vs redb: an object graph against 54 tables and Include
items.summary: An employee with addresses, contacts and dictionaries: 54 tables and 31 Include calls in EF Core, one class in redb Pro. Measured on 100k objects: who wins where One employee from our examples takes 62 SQL queries and almost two seconds to read in EF Core. In redb Pro the same employee, from the same data and in the same shape, takes 131 ms and nine queries, and 36 ms and five on the repeat run. The difference is not that one engine is "fast" and the other "slow". It is how many tables have to be put back together to get one business object out of the database. Below: what exactly we compared, why a graph is expensive in normal form, how redb Pro learned to read it without folding everything, and where EF Core is simply faster. There are quite a few such places, and they are in the tables too. Every measurement uses one model from the examples project. items.title: Node.js Payment Reconciliation: Bounding Poison Retries Before Dead Letter Redrive
items.summary: Consider this proposed page for an e-commerce service: the nightly payment reconciliation deadline has passed, and background job queue retries still haven't produced a completed settlement batch. The Node.js worker keeps returning the same poison message for another attempt. The on-call sees its business date, an increasing attempt count, and the same validation error. A green dashboard would be little comfort. What page fired, and why did the system wait until the deadline to distinguish a payment-provider interruption from input that another retry cannot repair? TL;DR: Bound background job queue retries, send poison messages to a dead letter queue (DLQ), and record attempts and the last error outside the Node.js worker process. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so make reconciliation effects idempotent. Redrive only after correcting the cause, with a small, observable recovery batch. A queue receiving acknowledgments doesn't prove the payment ledger was reconciled. This is a proposed incident analysis, not a report of a measured outage. items.title: Smooth Page Transitions with the View Transitions API
items.summary: The View Transitions API lets the browser animate between two states of your UI without you hand-writing FLIP animations. Wrap the DOM update in document.startViewTransition: function showDetails(item) { if (!document.startViewTransition) return render(item); // fallback document.startViewTransition(() => render(item)); } The browser snapshots the old state, runs your update, then cross-fades to the new state by default. Give matching elements the same view-transition-name and they morph between positions: .card-image { view-transition-name: hero; } ::view-transition-old(hero), ::view-transition-new(hero) { animation-duration: 300ms; } Each name must be unique on the page at the moment of the transition. For classic multi-page sites, opt in on both pages: @view-transition { navigation: auto; } Respect users who prefer less motion with a prefers-reduced-motion media query. Keep transitions short (200-400 ms) so navigation never feels slower. Always keep the non-animated fallback path working. Progressive enhancement at its best: browsers without support just update instantly.

Then someone opens it on a phone and nothing happens, so touchstart and touchmove get bolted on, and now there are two code paths that drift apart. items.title: Horror color palettes and grading for animated Shorts (hex codes and code)
items.summary: Originally published on Homingo Learn. Dark is not the same as scary. A horror palette is a small set of colours with jobs: what feels safe, what is wrong, and how much of the frame the dark is allowed to take. Most horror palettes on the web are mood boards: five dark swatches and an adjective. They look right in a grid and go muddy in a video, because nothing says which colour goes where. This guide treats a palette as a set of roles, gives five palettes with hex codes, shows how to check them in grey, and grades the finished frame in Remotion or with ffmpeg. Roughly how much of the frame each role takes in a calm shot. The wrong colour is the smallest on purpose. Ground is the darkest colour: shadows and the dark itself. Lift it a little above pure black and tint it, so compression does not turn it into blocks. Mid is the room: walls, furniture, the far parts of the frame. It sits one clear step above ground. Safe is the light the characters trust: a lamp, a kitchen, daylight through a window. Usually warm. Wrong is the threat colour. items.summary: Originally published on the SharpQuest blog, written by Greg Kabacinski and Rutul Mehta from our .NET MAUI team. First published in March 2024 and updated for .NET 10, current tooling and the 2026 app store requirements. Key takeaways Microsoft ended support for Xamarin on May 1, 2024. Xamarin's last versions no longer meet Google Play and App Store requirements, so Xamarin apps can't ship updates. .NET MAUI is the successor to Xamarin.Forms: one project and one codebase for Android, iOS, macOS and Windows. Migrate to .NET 10 (MAUI 10), the current long-term support release. Before migrating, update the app to Xamarin.Forms 5 and current dependencies. There are two ways to migrate: a migration tool, or a new .NET MAUI project with your code copied in. We combine both. The .NET Upgrade Assistant is deprecated; the GitHub Copilot modernization agent in Visual Studio replaces it. Plan time for layouts, custom renderers and third-party packages. These take the most effort. .NET Multi-platform App UI (.NET MAUI) is the successor to Xamarin.Forms and Microsoft's framework for cross-platform apps with .NET. We started out 2 years ago building open-source developer tools (like Tach https://github.com/tach-org/tach), then pivoted to AI Search optimization, and are now focused on the intersection of the two spaces. items.title: I built a free, offline replacement for TORA that explains every simplex step
items.summary: For our Operations Research course at NMIMS Shirpur, my teammates and I wanted a tool that shows why each simplex step happens, not only the final answer. So I built OR/Studio: a free, open-source Operations Research workbench that runs in the browser and works offline. There are 13 solver modules: simplex (including Big-M, two-phase and dual), integer programming, nonlinear programming, transportation, assignment, network models, project planning, queuing, inventory, game theory, Markov chains, simulation and job sequencing. Every tableau and ratio test comes with a plain-language reason and the rule that was applied. In tutor mode you pick the entering variable and leaving row yourself and get told what went wrong if you're off. In diff mode you type your own working and it finds the first step where you diverged. Fractions are exact, so the numbers in a tableau match what you'd get by hand. Big-M and prohibited routes use a symbolic M, never a large number. The solvers are pure TypeScript with no UI dependency, and I tested them against independent checks, not against themselves: Linear programs against vertex enumeration and strong-duality checks on random instances. items.title: French Blood Banks Hit Alongside Cyberattack On European Supermarkets
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Reuters: The refrigerators at three regional blood banks in France were hit by a cyberattack overnight between Sunday and Monday, at the same time hackers struck supermarkets from Sweden to Belgium. "Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems," the health ministry said in a statement. The incident had no impact on blood supplies, EFS spokesperson Charley Dubois said. "We have staff round the clock since blood can be needed at any time. They were warned about the problems by alerts and moved the blood to other refrigerators that were not connected," she said. [...] Investigations are under way into how the attack was carried out, what equipment may have been affected and when systems can safely return to service. The attack followed a similar incident in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. items.title: Usestate in Reactjs
items.summary: Usestate UseState is one of the React Hooks used to manage state in a component. Normally, when we use a local variable, changing its value does not trigger a re-render of the component. But useState allows us to store a value and update the UI whenever that value changes. Using a normal variable doesn't trigger a re-render the UI still doesn't show anything about your process by using a normal variable. To overcome this using usestate updates changes in UI everytime when the component gets re-rendered. const [stateVariable, stateFunction] = useState(0); Statevariable -It stored the current state value. StateFunction - It is a setterfunction used to update the current state value. When called, it tells React to re-render the component so the UI can reflect the updated state.

items.title: Validate Telegram Mini App Raw initData in Express to Stop Front-End Identity Spoofing in React
items.summary: Imagine you are building an order checkout system inside a Telegram Mini App using React. When a user opens your application inside their mobile client, Telegram injects an embedded WebView context exposing the global window.Telegram.WebApp object. React developers often jump straight into building UI components by pulling user profile details directly from window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe.user. If you send this initDataUnsafe user ID directly to your API to look up accounts, process orders, or issue rewards, your application is completely vulnerable to identity spoofing. Because Mini Apps are standard web applications running inside an embedded browser frame, anyone can open your Mini App's URL in a standard desktop browser, open Developer Tools, and mutate window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to contain any target user ID. An attacker can easily impersonate administrators or drain balances belonging to other users. To secure your React Mini App, you must ignore initDataUnsafe for authorization and treat the raw window.Telegram.WebApp.initData query string as an unverified credential. items.title: useContext in React
items.summary: Imagine we are building a website with a dark mode feature. Multiple components may need to know whether dark mode is enabled or disabled. One way to share this data is through props. But passing props through many components can become difficult. React provides a hook called useContext to solve this problem. useContext is a React Hook that allows us to access shared data from different components without passing props manually through every level. In simple words, useContext helps components share data easily. Let's understand with an example. Imagine we have three components: App Profile User The App component has a username that the User component needs. We can pass the username through props: function App() { const username = "Lokesh"; return ; } function Profile({ username }) { return ; } function User({ username }) { return Hello, {username} ; } Here, Profile does not need the username for its own work. It only passes it to User. When we pass props through components like this, it is called prop drilling. For deeply nested components, prop drilling can make code difficult to manage. items.title: Opening a panel right under the text caret on macOS
items.summary: I'm building yabbistir, a clipboard history for macOS. Its one trick is where it opens: press ⇧⌘V and the panel appears 8 points under the text caret of whatever app you're typing in. You type to search, press ↵, and the item is pasted back into that app. Your eyes don't travel and your hands don't leave the keyboard. That needs three things macOS doesn't hand you directly: the caret's position in someone else's app, a sensible answer when that app won't tell you, a window that takes keystrokes without taking focus away from the app you're typing in. Here is how each one works, with code from the app, shortened. There's no "where is the caret" API on macOS. There is the Accessibility API, the one assistive apps like VoiceOver use to read other apps' interfaces. Your app needs the Accessibility permission for it (AXIsProcessTrusted() tells you whether you have it), and then it can ask three questions: Which element has keyboard focus? Ask the system-wide element for kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute. What's selected in it? kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute returns a CFRange. With nothing selected, it's an empty range at the caret. items.title: NASA's Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth
items.summary: joshuark shares a report from Wired: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft -- which is roughly as big as a large elevator -- will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low. The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered. The U.S. Space Force now expects Swift to reenter Earth's atmosphere around November 6. items.title: Cleaning duplicate photos inside Lightroom Classic and Capture One catalogs without breaking them
items.summary: Disclosure: I'm the developer of Folio Refresh, the Mac app this post is about. Most duplicate photo finders work on folders. Point them at a drive, they hash files, they move copies to the Trash. That is fine until the photos live in a Lightroom Classic or Capture One catalog. Delete a file behind Lightroom's back and the catalog shows a missing-photo badge; delete the wrong copy and you lose the edits, ratings and collections attached to it. When I built Folio Refresh I wanted it to clean duplicates inside those catalogs, so here is how it does that without corrupting them. A Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat) is a SQLite database. A Capture One catalog (.cocatalog) is a package with a SQLite database (.cocatalogdb) inside. Neither schema is documented, and both change between versions. That shapes every rule below. Scanning only ever opens the catalog read-only. Lightroom: SQLITE_OPEN_READONLY. SQLite guarantees a read-only connection cannot write the database or its log, so this is safe even while Lightroom has the catalog open; it is just another reader. items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.title: Dinosaur Blood Found In Fossils For the First Time
items.summary: Researchers have confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside the 115-million-year-old fossilized bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali from Brazil. The discovery challenges assumptions about how long blood-related biomolecules can survive and could help scientists study dinosaur metabolism, blood evolution and even how traces of ancient life might be preserved on other worlds. Popular Science reports: The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger. After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. items.title: Why your Mac stays awake after you close the lid: two sleep traps
items.summary: I make Vigil, a Mac app that keeps the machine awake for long jobs, even with the lid closed. Most of the work turned out to be the opposite problem: getting the Mac to sleep again afterward. Here are two traps I measured, and the commands to check your own Mac. Vigil holds the Mac awake with pmset disablesleep 1 and lets go with disablesleep 0. On 4 Sep I tested it on an M4 MacBook Air. I closed the lid at 20:27 and the hold ended at 20:42. At 22:50 the Mac was still awake, and hot, in a bag. pmset -g explained it: sleep 1 (sleep prevented by Claude, coreaudiod, powerd, sharingd, Sada) Lid-close sleep is a one-time event at the moment the lid closes. If something blocks it then, macOS doesn’t try again when the block lifts. All that’s left is idle sleep, and any app holding an idle assertion stops that too. The fix: when a hold ends while the lid is closed (AppleClamshellState is true), run pmset sleepnow as root right after disablesleep 0. Skip it if an external display is connected, because that person is using clamshell mode on purpose. .userInitiated quietly blocks sleep Sada, another of my apps, sat in that list above. items.title: Building a Private Photo Vault App for iPhone with No Account
items.summary: I build iPhone apps on my own. Secure Folder is the one I made for photos and videos I don't want in the camera roll. The vault stays on the phone. You don't sign up, and the photos aren't uploaded. The app doesn't use iCloud. I didn't want a login in front of a private photo. If the pictures lived on a server, someone could ask me to hand them over. The first launch is a 6-digit PIN for the vault. It isn't the iPhone passcode, so that passcode won't open these photos. Face ID or Touch ID can open the vault too, if you turn that on. The switch is in the Security tab. Auto-Lock is on by default, and it's one switch. There's no timer and no lock button. When the app leaves the screen, it locks. Coming back means the PIN, or Face ID if you turned that on. iOS keeps a picture of your app for the app switcher. If the cover waited until the app was fully in the background, that picture could be the last photo you had open. The blur goes up as soon as the app is no longer in the foreground. The lock follows when iOS has actually moved the app to the background. You can't turn the blur off, so the app switcher doesn't keep the last photo. People say "hide" and mean the file moved. Kansas elected its first Democratic U.S. senator in nearly 100 years (94 years to be exact), while Texas and South Carolina sent Democrats to the Senate for the first time in decades. Democrats also picked up seats in Ohio, Iowa, Maine, and North Carolina. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

This post covers how Kipzy gets those rules into every WKWebView without hurting launch time and without recompiling when a user turns blocking off for one site. All numbers below come from the real lists. The compile times were measured on an M3 Pro Mac, which uses the same content blocker engine as iOS. An iPhone is slower. WKContentRuleListStore.compileContentRuleList turns a JSON rule list into WebKit's compiled bytecode. It's fast for a few hundred rules. items.title: Action Runner iOS Architecture
items.summary: Around mid-2021, I'd started developing SwiftUI apps in a new way. I'd previously considered architectures like MVC, MVVM, VIPER, etc and many of them never felt right. I often found myself spending time considering where to put business logic. With SwiftUI, it wasn't entirely clear where data-level changes should be taking place. Most (or any?) business logic certainly shouldn't be living in the views, but should I be building controllers to manage data? When I did that, I ended up struggling to define the boundaries of each controller. Dependencies would start to get messy, and I'd start getting circular dependencies across controllers that called each other. Controllers would start to get really big, especially for authentication, and I'd often struggle to quickly find code I was looking for. Action? In my work using React, the one-way data flow in Redux and how it handled actions was an idea that came to mind to try to tame these large controllers I was noticing in my projects. items.title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool (9 minute read)

In the previous standard tool-calling model, agents could only perform single actions, but the exec tool allows them to perform multiple actions.

items.title: Knowing How Is Not Knowing What (14 minute read)
items.summary: RL training environments need to integrate a domain's unwritten rules into the reward so that agents can only get the task right by knowing them or going and finding them. Environments should be built as one world exposed through several surfaces. This allows you to pose the same task at different difficulties by changing the surface, and agents get a chance to learn when to switch. The reward also reads the world, so agents that go through different surfaces get the same outcome score if they reach the same authorized result.

items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
items.summary: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...
